detail:
Prediction: These Will Be AMD’s and Nvidia’s Stock Prices by 2028
Harsh Chauhan, The Motley Fool

NVDA
AMD
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) have experienced contrasting fortunes on the stock market in 2026, with one clearly outperforming the other.

Nvidia, the artificial intelligence (AI) pioneer, has had a forgettable year. Shares of the semiconductor bellwether have dropped 20% in 2026, as of this writing. The company's outstanding growth has been overshadowed by recent developments that led to the resignation of co-founder and ex-CEO Jensen Huang.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

On the other hand, AMD stock has surged 140% this year. The company's growing prominence in the AI chip market has boosted investor confidence in the stock, and it seems well-positioned to sustain healthy growth over the next couple of years.

We will examine AMD and Nvidia's prospects and valuations in this article to determine where their stock prices could be in two years.

Image source: Getty Images.

AMD's accelerating growth suggests more upside by 2028

AMD has been playing second fiddle to Nvidia in the AI data center graphics processing unit (GPU) market, but the shift in AI workloads from training to inference and agentic AI has created a huge tailwind for the company.

AMD sells both data center GPUs and server central processing units (CPUs), and the increase in demand for the latter has supercharged the company's growth. The chip designer's revenue increased by 45% year over year in the third quarter to $13.4 billion, and it is now forecasting a much stronger increase of 66% in its top line in the current quarter.

Server CPUs are playing a key role in this acceleration. AMD noted that its server CPU revenue more than doubled in Q3 compared to the year-ago period. The company was originally expecting an 80% increase in this segment. Looking ahead, AMD expects server revenue to increase by more than 100% in 2027, driven by the launch of its next-generation Venice processors.

AMD points out that its partners have committed to launch over 240 platforms based on the Venice CPU, which is 20% higher than the previous-generation Turin server CPU. Even better, AMD forecasts the server CPU total addressable market (TAM) to jump to $220 billion in 2030, a massive improvement over just $26 billion last year.

Additionally, AMD has been winning share in server CPUs. Mercury Research notes that AMD's server CPU share increased by 7.7 percentage points year over year in the third quarter to 35.5%. So, the company still has a lot of room for growth in server CPUs, which is one of the biggest reasons why its earnings per share (EPS) are predicted to more than triple between 2026 and 2028.

Key Takeaways

Arm shares fell 20% in a week in an AI chip selloff that also hit Nvidia and AMD.

Arm's own risk: Nvidia's recruiters reportedly approached CEO Rene Haas, who leads Arm's data center chip push.

Analysts expect Arm's EPS to more than double by fiscal 2029, and the stock trades below its average multiple.

I'd wait for Haas to say he's staying before buying the dip.

Arm Holdings (ARM:NASDAQ) fell 20% in the past week in a chip selloff that took Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) down 23% and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) down 21%.

But Arm has one risk of its own: Nvidia is reportedly courting its CEO, Rene Haas, to replace Jensen Huang.

A chip rout did most of the damage

Chip stocks fell on Monday, Nov. 16, on reports of tougher US limits on China's chip access and worry over Nvidia's leadership before its earnings. They kept falling after California's attorney general said Thursday that he had subpoenaed Nvidia over its former CEO.

Server demand looks fine, too. AMD's data center revenue rose 97% to a record $8.5 billion in its September quarter, led by the EPYC chips that Arm's new AGI CPU competes with.

Haas is the risk that's Arm's alone

The Financial Times reported on Nov. 13 that Nvidia's board had approached Haas. On Wednesday, Bloomberg reported that Nvidia's recruiting firm had approached him too, though Nvidia hasn't made a formal offer.

That's a problem, since Haas is the one selling Arm's data center plan, including $15 billion a year in chip revenue by fiscal 2031.

The business didn't change this week

Arm's fiscal second quarter was a record: revenue rose 27% to $1.44 billion, and data center royalties doubled. Analysts expect normalized EPS to more than double from fiscal 2026 to fiscal 2029:

Arm Holdings (ARM): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2029 (years to March) (TIKR)

I don't see a chip selloff moving those estimates. A new CEO who rethought the chip plan could.

title: Jim Cramer Will “Thank the Shortseller for a Discount” on AMD. Is the China Risk Overblown?

Jim Cramer Will “Thank the Shortseller for a Discount” on AMD. Is the China Risk Overblown?

NVDA

Trading disclosure
Jim Cramer Will "Thank the Shortseller for a Discount" on AMD. Is the China Risk Overblown? ©Alexander's Images, Erik G from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

AMD fell 20% in two days, starting with an 8% drop after short seller Hunterbrook reported that a blacklisted Chinese server maker kept using newer AMD firmware.

The firmware is for EPYC server CPUs, and Hunterbrook says its findings don't prove an export violation.

The bigger risk is Washington, with a pause on a tighter blacklist rule ending Jan. 10.

Analysts kept raising AMD's revenue estimates up to the report.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) fell 8% on Thursday after Hunterbrook Media published "AMD Has Its Own China Problem." Its affiliate Hunterbrook Capital is short the stock. It fell 13% more on Friday, to $424.39, as tech sold off.

The title points to a real gap with NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ): AMD billed 22.4% of its 2025 revenue to China and Hong Kong, against 9.1% for NVIDIA, though NVIDIA's figure counts customers by headquarters.

Jim Cramer called it a "hitjob" on X and said he'd buy and "thank the shortseller for a discount back to where it was before that amazing quarter." I think he's right. The report is about EPYC server firmware, and two big AMD server builders, Dell Technologies (DELL:NYSE) and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE:NYSE), are growing their server sales fast.

AMD's China Problem Is a Server CPU Story

The Commerce Department blacklisted the Chinese server maker IEIT Systems in March 2025. Hunterbrook found that IEIT has since built at least six newer versions of AMD's startup firmware into its server updates, the latest posted Oct. 19 for EPYC Turin servers. It also found that three companies tied to IEIT sell AMD-based servers whose firmware is 99.94% identical to IEIT's: Maginfra in China, Kaytus in Singapore and Aivres in California.

But Hunterbrook says it doesn't know how IEIT got AMD's code or whether anyone held a license to supply it, and that its findings don't establish an export-law violation. AMD said the claims "misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships."

The business at stake is narrow, too. CNBC's John Fort said on Power Lunch that, by his read of AMD's 10-K, the export-restricted part is about $1 billion, mostly MI308 GPUs.

AMD's Estimates Kept Climbing

Cramer's "amazing quarter" was AMD's third, reported Nov. 3, when revenue rose 45% to a record $13.4 billion and Data Center revenue jumped 97%. Analysts expect revenue to nearly triple, from $34.6 billion in 2025 to $95.9 billion in 2027:

AMD Revenue, Actual and Estimates: 2023-2028 (TIKR)

That 2027 estimate was $89.2 billion in late October. I don't see much in the report that should move it, since the 2027 jump rests on Helios GPU racks for OpenAI and other big AI labs, and on a boom in server CPUs for AI agents.

Stanley Druckenmiller, David Tepper and 33 Other Big Funds Sold Advanced Micro Devices Last Quarter, While 21 Bought. Who's Right? ©Alexander's Images, Erik G from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Of 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30, 35 sold Advanced Micro Devices, including Stanley Druckenmiller's and David Tepper's, while 21 bought.

Fifteen of the sellers added Meta Platforms, which buys AI systems from both AMD and Nvidia, in the same quarter.

AMD trades at 28x forward earnings, below its five-year average of 34x, while analysts expect its earnings to more than double in 2027.

The buyers have the better case, since even the lowest analyst price target sits above today's price, though new export rules and a short seller's report are real risks.

Stanley Druckenmiller and David Tepper both sold every share of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD:NASDAQ) they owned in the third quarter. Plenty of big funds went the other way.

Of the 460 big funds that have filed 13Fs for the quarter ended Sept. 30 (funds readers know, or ones with $1 billion or more of US stocks, leaving out quant and index funds), 35 sold out of AMD or cut their stake by 20% or more. Another 21 opened a position or added 20% or more, and 76 held it at the quarter's end.

Fifteen of those sellers added Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) in the same quarter. Meta is one of the AI labs AMD is counting on for its Helios racks, and it's also planning a bigger rollout of Vera Rubin systems from Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ).

Druckenmiller and Tepper are out

Druckenmiller's Duquesne Family Office sold all 72,900 of its AMD shares, about $42 million at the Sept. 30 price, according to its 13F filed Nov. 16. That was a small bet, 1% of its 13F stocks at the end of June. Tepper's Appaloosa, which manages $20.4 billion, sold all 197,500 of its shares, about $115 million, after AMD made up 2% of its 13F stocks in June. Philippe Laffont's Coatue sold out too.

The biggest sale came from Parnassus Investments, which manages $41 billion: it cut its stake 38%, about $540 million of stock, though AMD was still its No. 9 holding. Cathie Wood's ARK Invest cut 52%, about $453 million, and Evergreen Quality Fund sold all 546,274 of its shares, about $317 million.

title: AMD Stock Just Plunged on a Short-Seller Report. Is This a Golden Buying Opportunity?
detail:
AMD Stock Just Plunged on a Short-Seller Report. Is This a Golden Buying Opportunity?
Prosper Junior Bakiny, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 1:50 AM MST 5 min read
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Chip stocks can't seem to catch a break. Recent developments, including a scandal and a major leadership change at Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), the most important semiconductor company, have weighed on the industry.

Another market leader is now facing a headwind. Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) was the target of a short-seller report published on Nov. 19, which sent the company's shares down significantly, extending the losses the chipmaker had experienced over the past few weeks. Is AMD worth investing in on the dip?

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Is AMD breaking the law?

Hunterbrook Media, an investigative journalism outlet, published the report in question. It is affiliated with Hunterbrook Capital, a hedge fund that trades based on reporting from its journalism arm.

In the report, Hunterbrook claims that some of AMD's firmware ended up in the hands of a Chinese server manufacturer that the U.S. government has blacklisted. That means AMD cannot sell its software to this company, at least not without the appropriate license or authorization, and may be in violation of export restrictions if it does so.

If AMD is found to have broken the law, it could face penalties, including a hefty fine, more stringent export restrictions, or, worse, criminal investigations involving its executives. This could disrupt the company's business for a while.

But that's if the allegations are true. Hunterbrook itself acknowledges that it doesn't know how this Chinese company got hold of AMD's firmware. It could have obtained the firmware in various ways that do not involve the company that made it.

There's also the possibility that AMD does have the appropriate export license. At any rate, there is limited direct evidence that demonstrates wrongdoing on the part of AMD, at least in my view.

Don't take your eyes off the ball

It's worth noting that AMD has denied these allegations. That's what the company would do, of course. It wouldn't simply acknowledge wrongdoing publicly. However, Hunterbrook Capital itself stands to gain from a decline in AMD's stock price.

That's how short-sellers make money. So there is also a financial incentive. Meanwhile, Reuters, a highly respected journalism outlet, said that it could not independently verify Hunterbrook's claims. That doesn't mean the claims are false.
